rows.subtype: Approach: weighing danger against being laughed at [Thinking]
rows.description: Dared to jump from a high wall, a boy imagines a broken leg against a moment of teasing, and decides that a few jokes will be forgotten sooner than an injury.

rows.subtype: Approach: predicting what could go wrong [Thinking]
rows.description: Before agreeing to walk on the railway track, a child asks what happens if a train comes or his foot slips, and the answers make the choice clear.

rows.subtype: Approach: accepting the dare to prove courage [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy climbs the tree over the pond because friends call him scared, and ends up stuck and scraped, showing how a wish for approval can outweigh good sense.

rows.subtype: Approach: regretting after joining in [Revision]
rows.description: After a friend gets hurt on a risky bicycle stunt, the boy admits he should have refused, tells his parents the truth and helps the friend, deciding to speak up early next time.

rows.subtype: Approach: gathering information from doctors first [Thinking]
rows.description: When a parent receives a serious diagnosis, the son asks the treating specialist to explain the stages, choices and unknowns, taking notes and avoiding decisions based on social media claims.

rows.subtype: Approach: assigning tasks among siblings [Action]
rows.description: The siblings divide roles: one handles hospital visits, one manages paperwork and insurance, one keeps relatives informed. A shared chat and weekly call keep everyone aligned.

rows.subtype: Approach: panic buying every suggested remedy [Pitfall]
rows.description: Anxious relatives push expensive unproven cures and the young adult, wanting to do something, spends savings on them. The family's money and energy drain without medical guidance.

rows.subtype: Approach: revising the plan after treatment response [Revision]
rows.description: When the first treatment plan brings side effects, the family talks with the doctor about changes, updates schedules at work and home, and adapts finances rather than sticking to the first plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition with a shared board [Action]
rows.description: A team of four splits the project into modules, puts tasks on a shared board with owners and dates, and reviews it briefly twice a week.

rows.subtype: Approach: dependency and critical-path thinking [Thinking]
rows.description: The team notices that the data pipeline must exist before model training and the interface can be built in parallel, so the pipeline owner gets support first.

rows.subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
rows.description: Confident that the project is easy, the team postpones coding until the final month, then finds integration bugs and rushes through a barely working submission.

rows.subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
rows.description: When a milestone slips twice, the team asks why repeatedly and finds that unclear requirements, not laziness, caused it. They write a one-page spec and agree on a definition of done.

rows.subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
rows.description: A student failing Maths asks why repeatedly and finds the trail leads back to weak fractions and algebra basics from Class 8, so the problem is foundations rather than the current chapter.

rows.subtype: Approach: seeking help from teacher or tutor [Action]
rows.description: The student stays back after class, shows the last three test papers to the teacher, and agrees on a twice-weekly doubt session, which is cheaper and more targeted than a full extra coaching batch.

rows.subtype: Approach: avoidance by studying favourite subjects [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student keeps revising English and Biology because they feel good, while Maths gets skipped. Marks in strong subjects rise slightly, but the failing subject continues to drag the overall result.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing no improvement and switching method [Revision]
rows.description: After a month of re-reading notes with little score change, the student admits passive reading is not working and shifts to closed-book practice questions, which quickly shows real weak spots.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.subtype: Approach: defining what AI may and may not do [Thinking]
rows.description: The team lead lists uses that are allowed, such as drafting tests and summarising public documents, and those that are not, such as pasting customer data or secrets into public tools.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.subtype: Approach: piloting on low-risk tasks first [Action]
rows.description: The team tries AI tools on documentation and unit test drafts for a month, measures time saved and error rates, and only then considers wider use in critical code.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.subtype: Approach: trusting output without review [Pitfall]
rows.description: A junior developer merges AI-written code without reading it. The code contains an insecure query, which passes basic tests and reaches production before a reviewer notices.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.subtype: Approach: incident review after an AI-related error [Revision]
rows.description: When an AI-generated report included a wrong number, the team traced how it passed review, added a verification step and updated the policy, treating the tool as a fallible colleague.

rows.subtype: Approach: pausing before replying [Thinking]
rows.description: After a harsh post about a product, the founder waits a day, aware that an angry reply written in the moment usually makes things worse and spreads the post further.

rows.subtype: Approach: taking the conversation to private channels [Action]
rows.description: For a customer-specific complaint, the company offers a direct call or email for details and returns later to say the matter was resolved, protecting privacy and avoiding a public fight.

rows.subtype: Approach: replying publicly and defensively [Pitfall]
rows.description: The founder argues point by point with critics and attacks their motives. Screenshots circulate, and the argument draws far more attention than the original complaint.

rows.subtype: Approach: using legal remedies only for real harm [Revision]
rows.description: When some posts contain false and harmful claims, the person collects screenshots and consults a lawyer about lawful options, but does not threaten critics over honest disagreement.
